To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the liver is a major organ for synthesis and cation of plasma proteins, (2) plasma proteins are important for drug distribution and elimination and may be involved in drug-drug interactions, (3) binding to plasma proteins may be altered in disease and (4) knowledge of the unbound drug concentration may be important in drug therapy.

the liver is a major organ for drug metabolism and elimination, but that it also plays an important role in the synthesis and cataboism of plasma proteins and that these processes can influence each other.

the liver has a remarkable capacity to efficiently remove drugs from the circulation despite extensive protein binding and that the interpretation of drug levels and dosage regimens may benefit from determination of drug-protein binding and the unbound concentration of the drug.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the influence of plasma proteins on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of drugs, the role of plasma proteins in the development of drug-drug interaction and the influence of disease states on plasma protein binding of drags and drug-drug interaction.
the role of plasma proteins in drug distribution and elimination and the consequences of changes in protein binding of drags for their pharmacokinetics.
the elucidation of the mechanisms of drug binding to plasma proteins and the influence of binding to plasma proteins on the hepatic clearance of drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the liver is a major organ of elimination of drugs and that the unbound drug concentration is a better predictor for the drug effect than the total plasma concentration.

the liver can remove drugs bound to plasma proteins, and that the unbound drug concentration in steady-state is a more important determinant of pharmacological effects than the total drug concentration in plasma.
protein binding does not necessarily alter drug clearance and distribution volume in the same way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the liver is a major clearance organ for drugs, that the liver can efficiently clear drugs that are highly protein bound, and that the liver can remove drugs from plasma even if they are highly protein bound.
the liver is an efficient organ for removal of drugs, even when the drags are extensively bound to plasma proteins.
the unbound fraction of drugs should be determined in order to predict the effects of protein binding on drug distribution, elimination and the interpretation of plasma concentration data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, although albumin and α 1 -acid glycoprotein are the most studied proteins in terms of their binding properties with drugs, there are other plasma proteins that are also capable of binding to drugs.
the liver is able to efficiently clear drugs, even when they are extensively bound to plasma protein.
protein binding of drugs is not a barrier to hepatic extraction.
